title: RAG, Vectors & Graphs
subtitle: How systems find evidence, connect facts, and ground answers
footer: Use frame navigation to follow the retrieval mechanism. The outline.md file is the reading surface on smaller screens.

bands.heading: RAG means relevance-selected evidence
bands.deck: A generation architecture, not a synonym for every external tool call

visual.thesis: RAG is an architecture for relevance-selected evidence, not a synonym for every tool call.
visual.focus: Question → candidate space → selected evidence → grounded answer
visual.caption: A query filters a large collection down to a compact context bundle.
visual.explanation: RAG ranks a large candidate space by relevance, then places selected passages beside the question so generation is constrained by evidence.
visual.example: Rank handbook sections for a PTO question and cite the matching passage instead of guessing.
visual.tradeoff: A keyed lookup or action tool can return text without ranking evidence.
visual.inspect: rank(query, corpus) then cite selected ids

bands.heading: RAG versus a generic tool call
bands.deck: The same call-and-return mechanics can serve different architectural roles

visual.thesis: Shared plumbing is not the architecture; only relevance search selects evidence.
visual.focus: Lookup, relevance search, and action sit on different roles
visual.caption: Only the middle path chooses evidence from a large candidate space.

nodes.label: Known lookup
nodes.note: Fetch one current value by a known key

nodes.label: Relevance search
nodes.note: Rank a large space and keep the best evidence

nodes.label: Action tool
nodes.note: Create, update, or trigger a side effect

visual.explanation: A retrieval step is RAG when it searches a large knowledge space, selects by relevance, and grounds generation. Fetching a known row or invoking a capability is a different role.
visual.example: Employee 4821's vacation balance is a keyed lookup; which PTO rule applies is a relevance search.
visual.tradeoff: Returning text from a tool does not make the call RAG if no ranking occurred.

bands.heading: Three questions that look alike
bands.deck: The user's wording does not tell you the architecture; the retrieval role does

bands.heading: Two pipelines, one handoff
bands.deck: Offline preparation shapes what the online answer can recover

visual.thesis: Offline preparation decides what the live question can recover later.
visual.caption: Indexing work and live retrieval meet at one evidence handoff.
visual.explanation: Sources are split and stored as vectors with metadata. At query time the question is embedded in the same space, then selected evidence is assembled for generation.
visual.example: A policy PDF is chunked overnight; a morning question retrieves those chunks instead of rereading the file.
visual.tradeoff: Bad splits or stale embeddings cannot be repaired by a clever prompt at answer time.

nodes.note: Create focused chunks without cutting meaning in half

bands.heading: A vector is a point in meaning space
bands.deck: Text becomes geometry so related ideas can be found without matching words

visual.thesis: A vector is a learned position so nearby text can match without shared wording.
visual.focus: Text → chunk → embedding → neighborhood → top K
visual.caption: Documents sit by semantic proximity; the query reveals its nearest neighbors.
visual.explanation: Each chunk is mapped to a numeric position that represents meaning, so paraphrases can rank above unrelated exact wording.
visual.example: A leftover-vacation query can retrieve a PTO accrual paragraph that never says leftover.
visual.tradeoff: Geometry is learned; rare identifiers still need lexical backup.

bands.heading: Chunking controls signal quality
bands.deck: The chunk is the unit of retrieval, context, cost, and possible confusion

visual.thesis: The chunk is the unit of retrieval, context cost, and possible confusion.
visual.focus: Too small versus too large, with a balanced start
visual.caption: Split size decides whether a hit carries enough meaning without mixing topics.

nodes.label: Too small
nodes.note: Precise signal, missing surrounding meaning

nodes.label: Balanced start
nodes.note: Near 800 characters with overlap and heading respect

nodes.label: Too large
nodes.note: More context, weaker focus, mixed topics

nodes.label: Tune
nodes.note: Judge splits against real retrieval tests

visual.explanation: Tiny chunks orphan the why; huge chunks mix topics and dilute the vector. Start near 800 characters with overlap, then tune against retrieval tests.
visual.example: A 120-character fragment citing see section 4 cannot explain the policy; a 4-page chunk buries the clause.
visual.tradeoff: Overlap helps continuity but multiplies storage and near-duplicate hits.
visual.inspect: compare chunk sizes against retrieval hits

bands.heading: Retrieval has several quality dials
bands.deck: A good answer depends on both the search space and the amount of evidence returned

visual.caption: Metadata filters, similarity, top-k, and rerank are independent controls.

nodes.label: Embed query
nodes.note: same vector space

nodes.label: Filter metadata
nodes.note: source, date, tenant

nodes.label: Choose Top K
nodes.note: too few or too many

nodes.label: Rerank
nodes.note: drop weak evidence

visual.explanation: Embedding the question is only the start. Metadata filters shrink the candidate set, top-k sizes context, and reranking prefers similar, useful passages.
visual.example: A tenant filter removes another team's docs; raising k from 4 to 20 can bury the right clause.
visual.tradeoff: Wide recall without rerank floods the window; tight filters can hide the only source.

bands.deck: The same database can support RAG or lookup depending on the query's purpose

nodes.label: Postgres + pgvector
items: Useful when relational data already dominates

nodes.label: Qdrant

bands.heading: Graph databases model connections directly
bands.deck: The answer may depend on a path through entities, not on the nearest paragraph

visual.thesis: Some answers live on named paths between entities, not in nearest paragraphs.
visual.focus: Entity → relationship → properties → traverse → impact path
visual.caption: A question follows directed links to connected evidence across hops.
visual.explanation: Graph retrieval stores entities and typed links. A question starts at a known node and walks those links, so the answer can be a path rather than a nearby paragraph.
visual.example: Which services fail if billing-db dies? is answered by traversing depends_on links.
visual.tradeoff: If the relationship is missing, traversal cannot invent the path prose might mention.

nodes.label: Relationship

nodes.label: Properties

nodes.label: Traverse

nodes.label: Impact path

bands.heading: One question can fan out across evidence types
bands.deck: A retriever can use several paths, then return one curated context

visual.thesis: One question can route across several retrievers, then return one curated bundle.
visual.focus: Question → hub → specialized retrievers → reconciled bundle
visual.caption: Vector, graph, keyword, and current-state paths merge after fan-out.
visual.explanation: A retriever hub chooses which evidence paths can answer this question, then merges vector, graph, keyword, and current-state hits before they occupy context.
visual.example: Who owns billing-db and what is replica lag? fans out to graph plus a live lookup.
visual.tradeoff: Fan-out raises recall and cost; without merge rules the prompt fills with overlapping fragments.

bands.heading: Vector, graph, keyword, hybrid
bands.deck: Each mechanism answers a different relevance question

visual.thesis: Each retrieval mechanism answers a different relevance question.
visual.focus: Four relevance questions on one field
visual.caption: Meaning, path, exact wording, and blended signals occupy different regions.

nodes.label: Vector search
nodes.note: Find themes and paraphrases by meaning

nodes.label: Graph search
nodes.note: Follow explicit entities and dependencies

nodes.label: Keyword / BM25
nodes.note: Protect identifiers and rare exact phrases

nodes.label: Hybrid
nodes.note: Combine signals, then rerank and curate

visual.explanation: Vector search recovers paraphrases. Graph search follows typed links. Keyword ranking protects exact names. Hybrid blends those signals and reranks.
visual.example: A product code SKU-9F2 needs BM25; a why-did-this-break question often needs graph plus vector.
visual.tradeoff: One mechanism for every question either misses identifiers or wastes traversal on prose.

bands.heading: From raw hits to usable context
bands.deck: Retrieval is not finished when results arrive; context still needs editorial work

visual.thesis: Hits are not context; editorial work turns candidates into a usable prompt.
visual.caption: Each step removes noise and preserves a trail the answer can cite.
visual.explanation: Hits still contain duplicates and weak matches. Deduplicate, rerank, then add source-aware instructions and an honest fallback.
visual.example: Twelve near-duplicate handbook chunks collapse to two sections plus a cite-or-refuse rule.
visual.tradeoff: Skipping editorial work spends the window on repeats.

nodes.note: passages and scores

nodes.label: Deduplicate
nodes.note: drop overlap

nodes.label: Rerank
nodes.note: keep useful hits

nodes.label: Guardrails
nodes.note: cite or refuse

bands.heading: The litmus test: retrieve or look up?
bands.deck: Ask whether the system chooses relevant evidence or fetches known state

nodes.label: Is there a large knowledge space?
nodes.note: Many candidate documents, chunks, nodes, or passages could answer

nodes.label: Does the step select relevance?
nodes.note: Similarity, traversal, filtering, lexical ranking, or reranking

nodes.label: Does the result ground generation?
nodes.note: The model should use external evidence rather than rely on memory

nodes.label: Is the source trail useful?
nodes.note: A good RAG result lets a reader inspect where the claim came from

nodes.label: Or is it known state?
nodes.note: Fetch a row, check a balance, read a price, or call an action

nodes.label: If unsure, name the role
nodes.note: The mechanism can look identical; the architectural purpose decides

bands.heading: Choose memory by question shape
bands.deck: Use the simplest retrieval strategy that answers the question well

visual.thesis: Pick the simplest memory that matches the question's shape.
visual.focus: What kind of request is this?
visual.caption: Document, relationship, hybrid, and lookup needs radiate from one decision hub.
visual.explanation: Route by question shape: explanations use vector or keyword retrieval, dependencies use graph, mixed needs use hybrid, and known values stay on lookup.
visual.example: Refund policy uses vector search; who owns billing-db uses graph; replica lag uses lookup.
visual.tradeoff: Defaulting every request to hybrid adds latency without helping a keyed status read.

nodes.label: Document or explanation
nodes.note: Vector or keyword retrieval over passages

nodes.label: Relationship or dependency
nodes.note: Graph traversal from a known entity

nodes.label: Meaning plus structure
nodes.note: Hybrid retrieval, then rerank

nodes.label: Known value or side effect
nodes.note: Direct lookup or an action tool

bands.heading: Keep the answer honest
bands.deck: The database is not the answer; evidence quality is the guardrail

visual.thesis: The store is not the answer; inspectable evidence is the honesty check.
visual.caption: Name the source, test the fit, refresh mutable state, and refuse a silent gap.
visual.explanation: Grounding fails when a citation cannot be named, the passage does not fit, or missing evidence is filled from model memory.
visual.example: If no handbook chunk supports a PTO claim, say the source is missing rather than invent a number.
visual.tradeoff: A fluent guess from weak neighbors still misleads; refusal is the honest completion.

nodes.label: Name the source
nodes.note: Show the document, node, path, or record

nodes.label: Test the fit
nodes.note: Reject irrelevant chunks and convenient weak matches

nodes.label: Refresh mutable state
nodes.note: Do not treat a static corpus as current

nodes.label: Admit a miss
nodes.note: Say what is unknown rather than filling from memory
